title: Spiritual Warfare
english: As we interact with our brothers, we must be experienced in war against those who oppose us.
The prophet's words remind us that even the meek can be warriors.
We should not think that the evil forces will calm down or that Satan's fury against us will cease.
In fact, the Bible says that if the Ethiopian can change his skin or the leopard its spots, then perhaps we can learn to do good, despite having learned evil.
The forces of evil surround our world, busy with each person's life, and they consider the saints with fierce eyes.
They tempt those who have already turned to evil towards even greater apostasy and worthlessness.
However, for those who choose to do good and boast in the righteousness of the upright, the forces of evil rise up in opposition.

Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the multitude of wicked demons and the innate law of the flesh, which is drawn towards what seems good to it and rises up hard against the spirit.

For our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the very wicked and rebellious multitude of demons, and also against the innate law of the flesh, which is drawn and forced towards what seems good to it, and rises up hard against the spirit.
The minds are opposed to each other, and they are divided, being very much opposed.
The souls of saints, it seems to me, suffer a similar fate to that of cities or regions when war is announced from outside, but inside the gates, there is no stability, only an innate battle raging.
This internal conflict is barely contained from the outside, and if there is any harmony, it is shattered by internal divisions.

The divine Paul testifies to this great difference in our desires, saying that he agrees with the law of God in his inner man, but sees another law fighting against the law of his mind and taking him captive to the law of sin in his members (Romans 7:22-24).
Thus, the war within us is twofold and not simple.
But, I think, someone might say that even these things I am saying are being refuted.

What then? Should we take up arms and give in to the enemies, yielding our necks to the violent as if to masters, knowing the danger of fighting and serving the flesh and demons, who have not experienced salvation?
By no means, for these are worthless.
Come, man, change your mind and take up courage; even if you hear the nature of the flesh, which is somewhat inclined towards pleasures, do not give in to the opposition.
The law of the flesh is lawless, drawing and forcing us towards what seems good to it, and rising up hard against the spirit.

The spiritual life is strengthened by small pains, and if one sees it beginning and being instructed by the desires of the Spirit, they should quickly cast away laziness and, imitating the best athletes, strip and warm up.
By being armed with the weapons of purity, one can show the pain from exercise, and the law of sin will flee, and they will see the fugitive, whom they thought was hard to capture.
The apostle Paul, being a commander of the desires of the flesh, said, 'I beat my body and enslave it, lest having preached to others, I myself become disqualified' (1 Corinthians 9:27).
Just as a proud horse is bridled for a knowledgeable run, so too the pursuit of spiritual discipline is in word.
The leaders of sailors persuade the ships to be steered straight by the turns of the helms.
A sober and renowned mind is least frivolous or easily deceived by cunning thoughts.
Having stood as if on itself and being unblemished, the mind harmonizes the flesh with the pains of exercise to will to submit to God.
It makes the journey through all deeds unerring, for the thoughts of the righteous are judgments, as it is written.

It would be truly unspoken that weakness is towards self-control, for not only is the manner of gentleness around the flesh, but the doubting in it has already been put to death and has been made ineffective through Christ.
As I reflect on my own life, I realize that I serve the law of God with my mind, but my flesh is still subject to the law of sin.
However, for those of us who are in Christ Jesus, there is no longer any condemnation, as long as we do not live according to the flesh (Romans 8:1).
The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death, which once held me captive.

This is because God sent His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and through Him, He condemned sin in the flesh, so that the requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk according to the Spirit and not according to the flesh (Romans 8:3-4).
As a result, the flesh has been put to death, as it were, in regard to its lusts.
For those who want to conquer their sinful desires, God gives them the power to do so.
We are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to its desires.
If we live according to the flesh, we will ultimately die, but if by the Spirit we put to death the deeds of the body, we will live (Romans 8:12-13).
All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God, and as such, they should not be slaves to the flesh, but rather guardians of virtue, preserving the glory they have found in Christ.
On the day of judgment, it will not be possible to make excuses for the times of laziness, saying 'I was dominated, I was a slave.'
Christ and the law of freedom will convict us, and will force our thoughts to be in opposition to such excuses.

The trainer of the saints should explain and teach us about our struggles in the flesh, writing in this way: I urge you, brothers, through the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, which is your rational worship (Romans 12:1).
We should not be conformed to this age, but rather be transformed by the renewal of our mind, so that we can test what the will of God is, which is good and perfect and pleasing.
As the wise John says, 'Do not love the world, nor the things in the world,' for if someone loves the world, the love of God is not in him (1 John 2:15).
Everything in the world, including the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not from the Father, but from the world.
The world is passing away, and its desire is also passing away.
However, the one who does the will of God remains forever.
Therefore, it would be foolish to prioritize the things of this world, which are fleeting and worthy of mockery, over the things that are truly important and lasting.
To achieve this, we must show ourselves to be superior to the miserable love of the flesh and strive for virtue, which is worthy of our effort.
This requires not only self-control over the body, but also the cultivation of gentleness of character and manner.
translator_notes: The Greek text is fragmented and ends with the phrase 'καὶ τῆς ἑτέρας ἐπιεικείας τῆς ἐν ἤθει καὶ τρόπ', which is cut off mid-sentence. The translation renders this fragment literally with a trailing ellipsis.

title: Gentleness and Compassion
english: The mind, having put on gentleness from self-control, is unenslaved to anger; for the one controlling anger is stronger than the one taking a city, as it is written (Proverbs 16:32).

Furthermore, the world in word is most youthful, and not inferior in unjust or superfluous acquisitions; considering righteousness to be without love of money, and voluntary poverty to be preferable to the abundance of wealth; for it is most necessary for the disciple of the Savior to be revealed, and truly existing, as the wisest Paul commanded, saying: Having food and shelter, we will be content with these (1 Timothy 6:8).
Those who want to be rich fall into many foolish desires, which plunge people into destruction and perdition.

Therefore, the pursuit of superfluous things should be avoided; and the use of more than necessary things should be rejected, as if into a boundary or a wave, and the use of necessary things should be preferred, I say, and cheap clothing; for this is the most profitable and trouble-free way to live, and having a trouble-free way of obtaining what is needed.

And besides all these good things, the law of brotherhood in Christ should be honored, and the rule of love for one another should prevail; for love is the fulfillment of the law, as it is written (Romans 13:10).
And we say that the fruit of love is to pity those in need and scarcity of necessary things; and to be nothing in word, but to have works that demonstrate our faith.

Do not say, man, to yourself: I have become rich in faith; I have known the natural and true God and Lord; I have turned away from devilish snares and demonic deceit; I have washed away the crimes of idolatry; and my boast of kindness is what saves me.
But remember the words of the one who says that faith without works is useless (James 2:26); if someone claims to have faith but does not have works to back it up, can they really be saved?
What good is it to tell someone who is naked and hungry to go in peace, to be warm and full, if we do not provide for their physical needs?

This kind of faith is not only unhelpful, but it also shows a lack of understanding of the divine laws that we are called to obey; and to be unlovingly presented, and to be nothing in word, is to reject the servitude of obedience to God's laws, which is to cast off the divine yoke, a difficult and dangerous thing to do.

Therefore, our faith must be accompanied by works, and we must strive to be merciful, just as our heavenly Father is merciful (Matthew 5:48); for judgment is merciless to one who has not shown mercy, and mercy boasts over judgment (James 2:13).

It is not difficult to demonstrate this from the sacred Scriptures, which reveal the rewards of loving one another and the condemnation of those who oppose such love; as the blessed Job said, 'I was not unable to meet the needs of those who had a need, I did not overlook the widow, I did not eat my bread alone, I did not refuse to give to the orphan, I did not despise the naked' (Job 31:16-21).

The rich man in the Gospels, who clothed himself in purple and fine linen, enjoying himself lavishly, is condemned and has unavoidable punishment; as the Savior tells the story, a certain poor man, Lazarus, was thrown at the rich man's gate, carried and desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table (Luke 16:20-21).
But even the dogs came and licked his sores; and ultimately, the poor man died and was carried away by the angels to Abraham's bosom, while the rich man also died and was buried.

In Hades, the rich man lifted up his eyes, being in torments, and saw Abraham and Lazarus in his bosom, and he himself, crying out, said, 'Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am suffering in this flame' (Luke 16:24).

Abraham responded by saying that the rich man had received his good things in life, while Lazarus had received the bad things; now he is comforted, but you are suffering; and the rich man had lived a life of luxury, with fine clothing, a magnificent house, and a large number of servants to cater to his every need, but he was without pity and insensitive, and thought it a burden to show kindness.

In contrast, Lazarus was a wretched poor man, without a home or relatives to care for him, and in desperate need of bodily comfort; he had to focus all his efforts on obtaining the basic necessities of life, and his well-being was measured in terms of a few simple things; and the human condition is one of necessity, where hope and prayer must come to an end in order to receive even the most basic necessities, such as bread and rags.

This is the state of wretchedness that the word of the evangelical parable describes, where one is forced to beg and has only dogs as companions, and is delighted to receive scraps from those who are serving; but the noble and compassionate man does not consider such things, for he is without pity and insensitive, and thinks it a burden to show kindness, and considers the tears of the afflicted to be a useless weight, and is not moved by their sufferings.

He is not concerned with the fact that he is no better than those who are in tombs, and is abhorrent and worthless, and is not considered to be of any account; nevertheless, one should consider that the creator and craftsman of our nature has not provided a different path to existence for the rich and the poor, but rather the same birth and death, and the same body, and the same heaven, and the same sun shines on all, providing equal light to all, regardless of their wealth or social status.

The natural world is not subject to corruption, nor is God, the creator of all things, but human greed has introduced this concept; perhaps, as we have recently discussed, there is no obstacle to understanding the divine intention, and we can see that the universe is governed by the principle of love, which leads to equality.

The one who distributes the goods of nature equally, without favoring anyone, would surely want to eliminate greed in others and appoint those who have more as stewards of those in need, so that they can share in the glory and delight that lasts forever; as the Savior says, 'Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful' (Luke 6:36); and let us remember the words of James, 'For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy; yet mercy triumphs over judgment' (James 2:13); and the word of the Lord says, 'What does it profit, my brethren, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?' (James 2:14).
Being in those things, we should strive to be merciful and to show kindness to those in need; for as the Savior says, 'Let us be merciful, as our heavenly Father is merciful' (Matthew 5:48).
translator_notes: The Greek text may be fragmented, and some sentences may be cut off at the beginning or end.
The translation tries to follow the original word order as closely as possible, but some adjustments were made to ensure natural and clear English prose.
The Bible references are not always exact quotes, but rather allusions or paraphrases of biblical passages.
The word 'ἀμελ[λ]ητὶ' is fragmented, but it is likely that it should be completed to 'ἀμελήτως', meaning 'without hesitation' or 'without care'.

title: Wealth and Piety
english: Lazarus, who was consumed by sores and death, was carried away by angels to Abraham's bosom.

In contrast, the rich man, who was excessively surrounded by wealth and flatteries, and was considered enviable and blessed, and his years were often regarded as superior, was handed over to the laws of nature and was swallowed up by the darkness of death.
Instead of earthly goods, he was exchanged for the judgment of Hades, paying the penalty of love of wealth.
This raises the question of how poverty, which has the boast of piety towards God and is valued by the law of righteousness, and has chosen the bitter vote for itself, can be considered a blessing.
Perhaps some would say that if poverty has chosen the bitter vote for itself, how can this be?

It is necessary to consider that wealth is often accompanied by many inappropriate things, and the rich are more prone to haughtiness and excess, while the poor are troubled and distressed, seeking to acquire something and find a moderate consolation for their needs.
In addition to all these things, it is necessary to consider how each person's manner influences the nature of their actions, shaping them according to their will, either for good or for ill.
Just as the beauty of an object can be enhanced by the application of dyes, so too can the nature of things be transformed by the manner in which they are handled.
The person who manages poverty wisely, for example, is truly the best of all, and I will say so without hesitation.
For if someone is content with little and has acquired the most necessary things through their own efforts, they offer prayers of thanksgiving.
How could they not be worthy of praise, having chosen a path of humility and self-control, and having rejected the ways of evil?

On the other hand, the person who is conspicuous for their abundance of wealth, and yet uses it to care for others and to alleviate the suffering of those in need, is truly justified in the eyes of God.
By overcoming and enduring the challenges of life, and by making temporary wealth a servant of their own pleasure, they demonstrate a profound understanding of what is truly important.

The story of the rich man and Lazarus comes to mind, where the poor man is rewarded with unexpected luxuries; the rich man, on the other hand, is punished with fire and torments, and his years, which were often named as better, are now filled with suffering.

If someone were to approach him at the most opportune moment and speak to him, asking to see how many possessions he might wish to sell in order to escape punishment, having chosen the better option, would he not readily agree to give up all his property for this?
It is foolish and ignorant to think that one can learn through experience to endure terrible things, and that this is possible for those who wish to have it outside of necessity and compulsion.
The Savior himself told us that unless our righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, we will not enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:20).
What then did the law given through Moses, which was a type and shadow, teach those in Jerusalem to honor the equality of brothers?

They, having despised the great and abundant manna, and having become hungry, were about to mourn the death of the all-wise Moses, and were saying that they could no longer be saved due to the overwhelming famine, and were already lamenting their funeral dirge, saying: 'Would that we had died, struck down in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots and ate bread to the full' (Exodus 16:3).
Moses, being very wise, did not know what to do or say.
But they, having hope only in God, showed the end of their expectation without hesitation.
The Lord then spoke to Moses, saying, 'Behold, I will provide bread from heaven, and the people will go out and gather their daily portion' (Exodus 16:4).

Moses interpreted the power of the law to the Israelites, explaining that this bread was a gift from the Lord, and that they should gather it, each one according to the number of people in their household, and collect it in their tents.
They did so, and surprisingly, the one who gathered much did not have more, and the one who gathered little did not have less.
This was because the Lord of the law did not allow them to gather more than they needed, only what was sufficient for that day's food.
If someone gathered more, the excess would be infested with worms, demonstrating that having just enough is pleasant and blameless, but storing up more than needed is a cause for worms.
The Savior teaches us to make friends for ourselves from unjust wealth, so that when we fail, they will receive us into their community.

The blessed Paul also understands this principle and applies it to the community of believers, saying that our abundance should be used to meet the needs of others, and their abundance should be used to meet our needs (2 Corinthians 8:14).
Let us be kind to each other, compassionate, forgiving each other, just as God forgave us in Christ.
We have been given forgiveness of sins and unfailing love, and we must strive to follow the calmness that is in God, the Master of all, and to forgive others, just as we have been forgiven.
This is not an easy task, as we are all prone to small-mindedness and failures, but it is necessary for us to grow in love and kindness.
If we were to grieve over every ordinary thing that happens, we would be deeply distressed, and our entire life would be filled with bitterness and sorrow.
Our lives would be marked by constant pain and sadness, and we would struggle to find any joy or peace.
The paths of those who are forgetful and vengeful lead to death, as it is written (Proverbs 12:28).
Nothing can stop each person's soul from being consumed by death, because they are unable to cry out against the pain in a noble way.
Instead, they are always being provoked to fiercely resist the things that have happened, and they are carried away by their emotions.
As the blessed Paul said, we should bear each other's burdens, and in this way, we will fulfill the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2).
This approach to piety is transparent and clear, and it is the key to living a life that is pleasing to God.
However, there are some people among us who are far from wanting to be good, and they take pride in their own soul's forgetfulness.
They consider it a great accomplishment to be able to forget the wrongs that have been done to them, and they look down on those who are not able to do the same.
If someone who is called to brotherhood stumbles slightly, they will condemn them completely, and they will be carried away by their uncontrollable impulses.
They will trample on others like a bull, thinking that the opinion of not doing anything bad is the most shameful thing.
They believe that unless they do every terrible thing, they are not truly living.
But if someone who has stumbled against them is stronger, they will be surrounded by many servants of savagery, and they will be in grave danger.
